### PERF-215 — BadanCard applies `.shadow()` unconditionally on every card instance app-wide

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `BadanCard` (the app's single card primitive, used dozens of times per screen — Home, Body pillars, Metric Detail, Settings, Timeline) unconditionally applies `Modifier.shadow(elevation = 6.dp, ...)`, which forces Compose to allocate an off-screen compositing layer per card.
- **Recommendation:** Consider a cheaper elevation treatment (e.g. a static border/tint, or `graphicsLayer` with `renderEffect` only where truly needed) for the common case, reserving real shadow rendering for surfaces that need it most (e.g. modal sheets).
- **Why it matters:** Shadow is one of the more expensive per-node Compose modifiers; applying it to every card on screens with many cards (Home casual/power body, Body pillar list, Metric Detail) multiplies compositing cost.
- **Expected user impact:** Reduced GPU/compositing overhead and smoother scrolling on card-dense screens.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** Yes (visible visual change to every card in the app)
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/designsystem/components/Card.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Design system
- **Suggested owner:** Design, Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Compositing cost scales with card count on every screen; likely not the top bottleneck today but easy to defer indefinitely without measurement.
- **Implementation notes:** Measure with GPU rendering profiler before committing to a visual change; this is a design-system-level tradeoff, not a pure internal fix.

### PERF-216 — HomeScreen.loadMetrics issues an N+1 repo-query pattern per key metric

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `loadMetrics()` in `HomeScreen.kt` loops over four metric ids (RHR, HRV, steps, active energy) and, for each, calls `latestInterval()`, `latestBaseline()`, and `intervalRecords()` as three separate SQLite queries — 12+ small queries for one Home load, in addition to the readiness/sleep/meds/insight/events queries in the same `loadHomeData()`.
- **Recommendation:** Batch the per-metric reads into single queries keyed by an `IN (...)` metric-id list (or add repository methods that fetch "latest interval + latest baseline for N metrics" in one round-trip each) instead of looping with three calls per metric.
- **Why it matters:** Home is the app's default landing screen and is reloaded on every cold start, tab return (see PERF-211), and relevant profile change — its query count directly sets the floor on how fast "Today" can render.
- **Expected user impact:** Faster Home tab load, especially on tab-switch-heavy sessions.
- **ROI:** 4
- **Importance:** 4
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/home/HomeScreen.kt` (`loadMetrics`), `.../storage/repositories/MeasurementRepository.kt`, `.../storage/repositories/DerivationRepository.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Home tab / data layer
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Every additional Home-tab key metric added in the future linearly adds three more queries to an already-N+1 pattern.
- **Implementation notes:** Add `MeasurementRepository.latestIntervals(metricIds: List<String>)` and `DerivationRepository.latestBaselines(metricIds: List<String>)` batch variants using `WHERE metric_id IN (...)`.
- **First patch sketch:** Add a batched `latestIntervals(ids)`/`latestBaselines(ids)` pair to the two repositories using a single `IN (?, ?, ?, ?)` query each, then rewrite `loadMetrics()` to call them once instead of looping per id.

### PERF-217 — MetricDetailScreen recomputes `fullSeries(tz)` redundantly across sibling composables

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `MetricDetailData.fullSeries(tz)` (a `map`/`filter` over `intervals`/`derived`) is called separately inside `MetricDetailContent`, `ChartCard`, and indirectly again via `seriesWithin` for `ValuesTableCard` — the same derivation re-runs two to three times per composition pass with no caching.
- **Recommendation:** Compute `fullSeries(tz)` once with `remember(data, tz)` in `MetricDetailContent` and pass the resulting list down to `ChartCard`/`ValuesTableCard` instead of having each recompute it from `data`.
- **Why it matters:** Small on a single render, but compounds with every unrelated recomposition (period selector change, theme flip) since none of the call sites are memoized.
- **Expected user impact:** Smoother interaction with the metric detail's period selector and chart.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/metricdetail/MetricDetailScreen.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Metric detail screen
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Minor but compounds with PERF-213/214 on the same screen.
- **Implementation notes:** `val series = remember(data, tz) { data.fullSeries(tz) }` at the top of `MetricDetailContent`, threaded into `ChartCard`/`ValuesTableCard` as a parameter instead of `data`.

### PERF-218 — MetricDetailScreen allocates a new DateFormat per row, every recomposition

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `dateText()` in `MetricDetailScreen.kt` calls `DateFormat.getDateInstance(...)` fresh on every invocation; it is called once in `HeaderCard` and again per row (up to 14) inside `ValuesTableCard`'s `forEach`, with no `remember`.
- **Recommendation:** Hoist a single memoized formatter (keyed on `language`) with `remember(language) { DateFormat.getDateInstance(...) }` and reuse it across all `dateText()` calls in the composition.
- **Why it matters:** `ValuesTableCard` alone can allocate up to 14 formatter objects per recomposition, on a screen the user is actively scrolling/interacting with (period selector).
- **Expected user impact:** Reduced allocation churn/GC pressure while browsing metric history.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/metricdetail/MetricDetailScreen.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Metric detail screen
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Minor per-instance cost, but a repeated pattern across the app (see PERF-219–221).
- **Implementation notes:** Same fix shape as PERF-219/220/221; consider a single shared `rememberDateFormatter(language, style)` composable utility used everywhere instead of fixing each screen ad hoc.

- **Affected systems:** Medication log screen
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile

### PERF-220 — TimelineScreen rebuilds SimpleDateFormat per call inside LazyColumn item composables

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `formattedDate()` and `timeText()` in `TimelineScreen.kt` each construct a fresh `SimpleDateFormat` (via `DateFormat.getBestDateTimePattern` + `SimpleDateFormat(pattern, locale)`) on every call; both are invoked per timeline day/event inside the screen's `LazyColumn items(days, key = ...)` list.
- **Recommendation:** Memoize both formatters per `(language, tz)` pair once above the list (e.g. `remember(env.language, tz)`), and pass the cached formatter into the day/event row composables.
- **Why it matters:** Unlike the other screens in this cluster, TimelineScreen is the one place already using `LazyColumn`, so as the user scrolls, every newly-composed row re-triggers this allocation — it is the item most likely to show up in a scroll-jank profile.
- **Expected user impact:** Smoother Timeline scrolling.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/timeline/TimelineScreen.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Timeline screen
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Timeline is the one list-heavy, scroll-driven screen in the app — this is its most direct scroll-jank risk.
- **Implementation notes:** `remember(env.language) { ... }` around both formatter constructions, hoisted above the `LazyColumn`.

- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2

### PERF-222 — BodyAllMetricsBrowser re-filters/regroups/sorts the full registry on every recomposition

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** In `BodyScreen.kt`'s `BodyAllMetricsBrowser`, `results`/`groups` (a `search()` + `groupBy` + `sortedBy` over up to 44 metrics) is computed inline in the composable body from `query`, with no `remember(query)` or `derivedStateOf` — it re-runs on every recomposition, not just on actual query changes.
- **Recommendation:** Wrap the filter/group/sort pipeline in `remember(query) { ... }` (or `derivedStateOf` if it should also skip recomposition when the derived result is unchanged).
- **Why it matters:** Negligible at 44 metrics today, but this is exactly the code path that scans/regroups on every keystroke and on every unrelated recomposition of the browser (e.g. theme flip), which will matter more as the metric ontology grows.
- **Expected user impact:** Smoother typing in the metric search field.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/body/BodyScreen.kt` (`BodyAllMetricsBrowser`)
- **Affected systems:** Body tab / metric browser
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Cost scales linearly with the registry size (`packages/metric-ontology/registry.json`), currently small but not fixed.
- **Implementation notes:** `val groups = remember(query) { ... }` around the existing `results`/`groupBy`/`sortedBy` chain.

### PERF-223 — BodyScreen.makePillar issues redundant DB queries trying candidate metrics serially

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `makePillar()` builds an ordered candidate list per family (headline metrics + all baseline-eligible metrics in the family) and calls `recentSeries()` for each candidate in a `for` loop until one returns data — each attempt, including ones that get discarded, issues its own chain of repository queries via `recentSeries`.
- **Recommendation:** Short-circuit earlier where possible (e.g. check `latestInterval`/`latestDerivedSeries` existence cheaply before pulling a full windowed series), or cache per-family "which metric actually has data" so repeat loads (post PERF-211 fix) don't redo the trial-and-error.
- **Why it matters:** The Body tab's pillar list is core navigation, loaded on every visit; wasted trial queries add avoidable latency to a frequently-visited screen.
- **Expected user impact:** Faster Body tab load.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/body/BodyScreen.kt` (`makePillar`, `recentSeries`)
- **Affected systems:** Body tab
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-211 (tab-switch caching reduces how often this cost is paid)
- **Risk if skipped:** Cost scales with the number of families × candidate metrics per family as the ontology grows.
- **Implementation notes:** A cheap existence check (`EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM ... LIMIT 1)`-style repository method) before committing to a full windowed fetch would cut most wasted work.

### PERF-224 — recentSeries/derivedSeries filter windows in Kotlin instead of at the SQL layer

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `derivedSeries()` in `BodyScreen.kt` calls `env.derivation.latestDerivedSeries(metricId)` (which has no date-range parameter and returns the metric's *entire* history) and then applies `.filter { it.first >= from }` in Kotlin.
- **Recommendation:** Add a ranged variant to `DerivationRepository` (`latestDerivedSeries(metricId, from, to)`) that applies the date filter in the SQL query itself.
- **Why it matters:** As a metric's derived-value history grows (it is append-only per PERF-235), every Body-tab pillar load fetches strictly more rows than it needs and discards most of them in application code.
- **Expected user impact:** Body tab load time stays flat as history grows instead of degrading.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/body/BodyScreen.kt`, `.../storage/repositories/DerivationRepository.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Body tab / data layer
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-234, PERF-235
- **Risk if skipped:** Query cost grows unbounded with total derived-value history, not with the visible window.
- **Implementation notes:** Extend the existing `latestDerivedSeries` SQL with an optional `AND d.period_key >= ? ...` — period keys are lexicographically sortable `day:YYYY-MM-DD` strings so a range filter is a straightforward string comparison.

### PERF-225 — Non-lazy Column+forEach used for lists that will grow

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `BodyAllMetricsBrowser`, `LogHubScreen`'s recents row, `SourcesScreen`'s device list, and `MedicationLogScreen`'s regimen list all render their items via a plain `Column` + `.forEach`, not `LazyColumn`/`LazyRow` — every item composes eagerly regardless of scroll position, unlike `TimelineScreen` which already uses `LazyColumn`.
- **Recommendation:** Convert these to `LazyColumn`/`LazyRow` with stable `key = { it.id }` so off-screen items aren't composed.
- **Why it matters:** Bounded and cheap at MVP data volumes (a handful of regimens/devices, 44 metrics), but each of these lists is user-generated-content-shaped and has no cap — a power user with many medications or a large search result set will pay for eager composition.
- **Expected user impact:** Consistent performance regardless of how much data a user accumulates.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/body/BodyScreen.kt`, `.../features/loghub/LogHubScreen.kt`, `.../features/body/SourcesScreen.kt`, `.../features/medication/MedicationLogScreen.kt`
- **Affected systems:** List rendering
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Degrades gracefully at small scale but is a real risk for long-term/power users, which BADAN's local-first, no-limits data model explicitly invites.
- **Implementation notes:** Straightforward mechanical conversion; verify nested-scroll interactions (these lists currently live inside an outer `verticalScroll` Column) before converting, since a `LazyColumn` inside a scrollable `Column` needs a fixed height or `Modifier.heightIn`.

### PERF-226 — Manual chunked(2) grids forgo LazyVerticalGrid's windowing

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `HomeScreen.MetricGrid` and `LogHubScreen`'s `TileGrid` hand-roll a two-column grid via `metrics.chunked(2).forEach { Row { ... } }` inside a `Column`, instead of `LazyVerticalGrid`, so every cell composes immediately with no windowing.
- **Recommendation:** Replace the manual chunked-row pattern with `LazyVerticalGrid(columns = GridCells.Fixed(2))` where it doesn't conflict with the outer scroll container (or use `userScrollEnabled = false` + fixed height if nested inside an existing scroll).
- **Why it matters:** Bounded today (4 Home metrics, a handful of log tiles) but the same pattern will not scale if the grid ever grows (e.g. more Home key metrics become configurable).
- **Expected user impact:** No visible change today; protects against future regressions as grids grow.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/home/HomeScreen.kt` (`MetricGrid`), `.../features/loghub/LogHubScreen.kt` (`TileGrid`)
- **Affected systems:** Grid rendering
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Low today; matters if Home's key-metric grid becomes user-configurable with more entries.
- **Implementation notes:** `LogHubScreen`'s `TileGrid` wasn't fully read in this audit — verify its exact implementation matches this pattern before converting (comment in file cites "the app's navigation has no dedicated browser route" style manual layouts elsewhere too).

### PERF-227 — StatefulContainer resets to Loading on every LaunchedEffect key change, discarding prior data

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `HomeScreen`, `MetricDetailScreen`, and `InsightsScreen` all set `state = LoadState.Loading` immediately before reloading inside their `LaunchedEffect(keys) { state = LoadState.Loading; state = withContext(IO) { load(...) } }` blocks, so any key change (e.g. toggling casual/power depth, switching language) flashes a full loading spinner even though the previous data is still valid to show while the reload happens.
- **Recommendation:** Keep showing the previous `LoadState.Loaded` value while a reload is in flight (e.g. a `isRefreshing` boolean alongside the last-loaded value) instead of transitioning through `Loading` on every key change.
- **Why it matters:** A depth/language toggle is a common, fast interaction (Settings → flip a switch) that currently produces a jarring full-screen spinner flash on every screen that's mounted, purely from re-fetching data that in most cases barely changes.
- **Expected user impact:** Smoother, flicker-free response to depth/language changes.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/home/HomeScreen.kt`, `.../features/metricdetail/MetricDetailScreen.kt`, `.../features/insights/InsightsScreen.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Loading-state UX / recomposition
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Every depth/language toggle continues to read as a slow, flickery interaction even once the underlying queries are fast.
- **Implementation notes:** Extend `LoadState` (or add a parallel flag) to distinguish "no data yet" from "have data, refreshing" so `StatefulContainer` can keep rendering the stale content during a reload.

### PERF-228 — BadanTheme.colors read broadly, widening the recomposition surface on theme/RTL flips

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** Nearly every composable in the app (`HomeScreen`, `MetricDetailScreen`, `BodyScreen`, design-system components, etc.) reads `BadanTheme.colors` at its own top level rather than receiving colors as a stable parameter, so a theme change (Settings → Appearance) or an RTL/LTR flip potentially invalidates every composable that reads it, not just the ones whose rendered color actually changed.
- **Recommendation:** Where colors are read many levels deep in a tree that itself doesn't otherwise need to recompose, consider narrowing the read to leaf nodes only, or confirm `BadanTheme.colors`'s underlying `CompositionLocal`/backing type is itself change-stable so downstream reads skip correctly (this needs verification against `designsystem/Theme.kt`, not fully audited here).
- **Why it matters:** Theme/appearance changes are rare user actions but touch the entire visible tree; whether that's cheap depends on how narrowly `colors` reads propagate, which is worth confirming rather than assuming.
- **Expected user impact:** Smoother theme-switch transitions if the current design turns out to over-invalidate.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/designsystem/Theme.kt`, and all composables reading `BadanTheme.colors`
- **Affected systems:** Theming
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-287 (compiler stability reports would confirm whether this is actually a hot spot)
- **Risk if skipped:** Unknown severity without measurement — flagged as a verification item rather than a confirmed regression.
- **Implementation notes:** Use Compose compiler metrics / Layout Inspector recomposition counts on a theme toggle before investing further here.

### PERF-229 — HomeScreen's single LaunchedEffect reloads the entire HomeData bundle for any of four unrelated key changes

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `HomeScreen`'s `LaunchedEffect(env.depth, env.language, env.profile.sensitiveModulesEnabled, env.profile.nutritionEnabled)` reloads *all* of readiness, sleep, key metrics, meds, insight, and events together as one `HomeData` object whenever any one of those four independent flags changes.
- **Recommendation:** Split `loadHomeData` into independently-keyed sections (e.g. metrics/sleep don't depend on `nutritionEnabled`; meds/events do) so a nutrition-module toggle doesn't re-run the readiness/metrics/sleep queries that have nothing to do with it.

- **Expected user impact:** Faster, more targeted Home updates when toggling individual modules in Settings.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/home/HomeScreen.kt` (`loadHomeData`)
- **Affected systems:** Home tab
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-216
- **Risk if skipped:** Minor annoyance today; becomes more noticeable once PERF-216's N+1 queries are fixed and the remaining cost is proportionally more about unnecessary re-triggering than raw query count.

### PERF-230 — InsightsScreen feedback tap rebuilds the entire insights list for a single-item change

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `InsightsScreen`'s feedback handler does `data.insights.toMutableList().also { it[idx] = it[idx].copy(feedback = newValue) }` and then `state = LoadState.Loaded(data.copy(insights = updated))` on every thumbs-up/down tap — a full list copy and a new `InsightsData`/`LoadState` object for a change to exactly one item.
- **Recommendation:** Model per-insight feedback as its own small piece of state (e.g. `mutableStateMapOf<String, Int>` keyed by insight id) read by each insight card, instead of copying the whole list through the top-level `LoadState`.
- **Why it matters:** Combined with PERF-213 (unstable `List` fields), this list copy invalidates recomposition-skipping for the entire insights feed on every single feedback tap, not just the tapped card.
- **Expected user impact:** Snappier feedback taps with no visible re-render of unrelated insight cards.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/features/insights/InsightsScreen.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Insights tab
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-213
- **Risk if skipped:** Minor in absolute terms (insight lists are short) but a reusable anti-pattern that will recur wherever a list item's state is mutated through a copied parent list.
- **Implementation notes:** A `mutableStateMapOf<String, Int>` for feedback, joined with the loaded insight list only at render time, decouples the write from the list identity.

### PERF-231 — Every repository read uses `SELECT *`, materializing unneeded columns per row

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** All bulk read methods across `MeasurementRepository`, `DerivationRepository`, `CatalogRepository`, `LoggingRepository` (e.g. `rawSamples`, `intervalRecords`, `sessions`, `allDerived`, `sources`, `regimens`) use `SELECT * FROM ...`, so `Row.from()` allocates a `HashMap` entry for every column of every row even when a call site only needs 1-2 fields (e.g. a sparkline only needs `value`).
- **Recommendation:** Add narrow projection variants (`SELECT metric_id, start_at, value FROM ...`) for the hot, high-frequency read paths identified elsewhere in this audit (Home sparklines, Body pillar series), reserving `SELECT *` for detail views that need full provenance.
- **Why it matters:** This is the concrete mechanism behind the architecture-level note that `query()` "materializes ALL rows into dictionaries keyed by column name" — every row pays for every column regardless of need.
- **Expected user impact:** Lower CPU/memory cost for the app's most frequent queries (sparklines, list previews).
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/repositories/MeasurementRepository.kt`, `.../storage/repositories/DerivationRepository.kt`, `.../storage/sqlite/Row.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage layer
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None

### PERF-232 — CatalogRepository.devices(sourceId) has no supporting index

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `source_devices` (`storage/Schema.kt`) has no index on `source_id`, but `CatalogRepository.devices(sourceId)` filters `WHERE source_id = ?` — every call (e.g. from `SourcesScreen`, and from `IngestionPipeline.upsertSourcesAndDevices` on every ingest) does a full table scan.
- **Recommendation:** Add `CREATE INDEX idx_source_devices_source ON source_devices(source_id);` in a new migration.
- **Why it matters:** Cheap and correct at MVP scale (few devices), but `upsertSourcesAndDevices` calls this once per descriptor on *every single ingest/sync call* (PERF-267), so the missing index compounds with sync frequency.
- **Expected user impact:** Faster Health Connect sync and Sources screen loads as device history accumulates.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/Schema.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage / catalog
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Negligible today; compounds with PERF-267 as sync frequency and device history grow.
- **Implementation notes:** Add as `Migration(version = 2, ...)` per the existing forward-only migration convention.
- **First patch sketch:** Add a new `Migration(2, listOf("CREATE INDEX idx_source_devices_source ON source_devices(source_id);"))` to `Schema.mainMigrations`.

### PERF-233 — baselines table's identity index isn't an ideal covering order for latestBaseline()

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `DerivationRepository.latestBaseline(metricId, context)` queries `WHERE metric_id = ? AND covariate_context = ? ORDER BY valid_from DESC LIMIT 1`, but the only supporting index is the 4-column unique index `idx_baseline_identity(metric_id, covariate_context, window_days, valid_from)` — since the query doesn't filter `window_days`, SQLite can use the first two columns but must still scan across `window_days` groups to find the true `valid_from` maximum.
- **Recommendation:** Add a dedicated `CREATE INDEX idx_baseline_lookup ON baselines(metric_id, covariate_context, valid_from DESC);` matching the actual query shape.
- **Why it matters:** `latestBaseline()` is one of the most frequently called reads in the app (Home, Body, MetricDetail, InsightEngine, BaselineEngine all call it), so its index quality matters disproportionately.
- **Expected user impact:** Faster baseline lookups across nearly every screen.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/Schema.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage / baselines
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Query cost grows with the number of distinct `window_days` values recorded per metric/context over time.
- **Implementation notes:** Add as a second statement in the same `Migration(2, ...)` introduced for PERF-232, since both are simple additive index migrations.
- **First patch sketch:** Add `Migration(2, listOf("CREATE INDEX idx_baseline_lookup ON baselines(metric_id, covariate_context, valid_from DESC);"))` alongside PERF-232's index in the same migration.

### PERF-234 — latestDerivedSeries's self-join re-scans the whole append-only table per call

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `DerivationRepository.latestDerivedSeries(metricId)` self-joins `derived_values` against a `GROUP BY period_key, MAX(computed_at)` subquery filtered only by `metric_id` — it re-scans and re-aggregates *every* derived row ever computed for that metric, not just the current display window, every time it's called (Home, Body, MetricDetail, Export all call it).
- **Recommendation:** Add an optional date/period-key range parameter (see PERF-224) so the subquery only aggregates the rows actually needed, and consider a covering index on `derived_values(metric_id, period_key, computed_at DESC)` (distinct from the existing `idx_derived_latest` which is already close but should be verified as the one actually chosen by the planner for this join shape).
- **Why it matters:** Because `derived_values` is append-only forever (PERF-235), this query's cost grows with total historical recomputes, not with the metric's true data volume — a slow-growing but real regression vector.
- **Expected user impact:** Query time for charts/sparklines stays flat over the life of an install instead of slowly growing.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No

- **Affected systems:** Storage / derived values

- **Risk if skipped:** Slow, compounding regression that won't show up in short-lived QA testing but will show up for long-term real users.
- **Implementation notes:** Pair with PERF-224's ranged-series repository method so both problems are fixed in one change.

### PERF-235 — derived_values has no compaction/pruning of superseded rows

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `derived_values` is append-only by design (INVARIANT I2) and every `recomputeAll()` call (every seed, reset, and Health Connect sync) appends a fresh row per period rather than updating in place; nothing ever prunes or archives rows that are no longer the latest for their `(metric_id, period_key)`.
- **Recommendation:** Introduce a periodic, safe compaction pass (e.g. move superseded rows to an archive table, or simply delete non-latest rows past a retention window) that preserves the audit trail requirement only as long as genuinely needed, or document/confirm that unbounded growth here is an accepted tradeoff.
- **Why it matters:** This table backs PERF-234's hot read path — every recompute silently grows the table that the app's most common queries have to scan through.
- **Expected user impact:** Sustained performance over the life of a long-running install instead of gradual degradation.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 4
- **Approval needed:** Yes (touches the append-only/audit-trail invariant, a deliberate architecture decision — any pruning needs product/architecture sign-off)
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/Schema.kt`, `.../storage/repositories/DerivationRepository.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage / derived values
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile, Product
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Very slow-motion regression; likely not visible for months of real usage, but real for a "keep forever" local-first app.
- **Implementation notes:** Any compaction strategy must preserve whatever audit/traceability guarantee I2 is meant to provide — this needs a product decision, not just an engineering fix.

### PERF-238 — SqliteConnection's single `@Synchronized` lock serializes unrelated concurrent reads

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** Every method on `SqliteConnection` (`execute`, `run`, `query`, `transaction`) is `@Synchronized` on the connection instance; since `database.main` is shared by every repository, two unrelated reads from different tables (e.g. Home's sequential `measurements`/`derivation` calls) still fully serialize through one JVM monitor even though WAL mode is designed to let readers proceed concurrently with writers.
- **Recommendation:** Evaluate whether the coarse lock is actually needed given `SQLiteDatabase`'s own internal thread-safety, or move to a narrower locking strategy (e.g. only guard `reopen`/`closeHandle` transitions) so concurrent reads aren't serialized by application code on top of WAL.
- **Why it matters:** This directly undercuts the benefit of enabling WAL in the first place (`enableWriteAheadLogging()` is called specifically so "bulk writes... are fast" and reads aren't blocked by writers) if a Kotlin-level lock re-serializes everything anyway.
- **Expected user impact:** Better concurrency for any future parallelized read pattern (e.g. fixing PERF-216/241/246/247 to run queries concurrently would need this to actually pay off).
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/sqlite/SqliteConnection.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage layer / concurrency
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Caps the ceiling on how much any future query-parallelization fix (PERF-241, PERF-246/247) can actually help.
- **Implementation notes:** Needs careful verification — Android's `SQLiteDatabase` has its own connection-pool/locking semantics that must be understood before removing the current lock; this is a "verify before changing" item, not a drop-in fix.

### PERF-241 — TimelineAssembler issues up to 7 fully serial repository calls per load

### PERF-248 — No WAL checkpoint / VACUUM strategy for either database

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** Both `badan.db` and `badan_sensitive.db` enable WAL (`enableWriteAheadLogging()`) but nothing in the codebase ever issues `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint` or `VACUUM` — the WAL file can grow across a long-lived install with frequent small writes (every settings toggle, every log entry, every derived-value append).
- **Recommendation:** Add a periodic (e.g. app-background-triggered) `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` and consider an occasional `VACUUM` given the append-only `derived_values` growth pattern (PERF-235).
- **Why it matters:** Left unmanaged, WAL file growth increases on-disk footprint and can slow down checkpoint-triggered stalls that Android's SQLite implementation performs automatically once the WAL crosses its default size threshold.
- **Expected user impact:** More predictable disk usage and fewer surprise stalls on long-lived installs.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/Database.kt`, `.../storage/sqlite/SqliteConnection.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage layer
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Slow-motion disk-usage and stall risk over the life of a long-running local-first install.
- **Implementation notes:** Trigger on `Activity.onStop`/process-lifecycle background transition rather than on a fixed timer, to avoid competing with foreground work.

### PERF-250 — No SQLite PRAGMA tuning beyond synchronous/foreign_keys

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `SqliteConnection.open()` only sets `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL` and `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` beyond enabling WAL — there's no `PRAGMA cache_size` or `PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY` tuning, leaving the default (relatively small) SQLite page cache in place for the scan-heavy queries flagged elsewhere in this section (PERF-234, PERF-244).
- **Recommendation:** Benchmark a larger `cache_size` and `temp_store = MEMORY` against the existing defaults on a representative low-end device before committing to specific values.
- **Why it matters:** A larger page cache directly reduces disk reads for the repeated full-table-ish scans this audit already identified; this is a cheap lever to pull once those scans are otherwise optimized.
- **Expected user impact:** Marginal query-latency improvement, most noticeable on the scan-heavy paths already flagged.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 1
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/sqlite/SqliteConnection.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage layer
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Minimal; a low-priority tuning pass rather than a fix for a specific observed problem.
- **Implementation notes:** Measure before/after on a low-end AVD profile (see PERF-299) rather than guessing at values.

### PERF-251 — No ANALYZE run after migration to inform the query planner

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `Database`'s `migrate()` never runs `ANALYZE` after applying the schema, so SQLite's query planner has no cardinality statistics for the composite indexes defined in `Schema.kt` and must fall back to heuristics for index selection.
- **Recommendation:** Run `ANALYZE` once after the initial migration (and optionally periodically thereafter) so the planner has real statistics once tables have meaningful row counts.
- **Why it matters:** Matters increasingly as tables grow past MVP-trivial row counts; negligible at today's data volumes.
- **Expected user impact:** Better query plans for the multi-index tables (`raw_samples`, `interval_records`, `baselines`) as data accumulates.
- **ROI:** 1
- **Importance:** 1
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/Database.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage layer
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Negligible today; lowest-priority storage item.
- **Implementation notes:** Trivial one-line addition once other storage fixes land; not worth a dedicated pass on its own.

### PERF-252 — CSV export renders the entire file into one in-memory string before writing

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `CsvWriter.render()` builds the full CSV (header + all rows) as one `StringBuilder`, and `ExportRunner.runCsv()` converts it to a `ByteArray` before a single `writeBytes()` call, rather than streaming rows directly to a `BufferedWriter`/`OutputStream`.
- **Recommendation:** Stream rows directly to the output file (e.g. `File(...).bufferedWriter().use { w -> w.write(header); rows.forEach { w.write(NEWLINE + line(it)) } }`) instead of materializing the whole file in memory first.
- **Why it matters:** For a multi-year, multi-metric "everything" export, this holds the full row list *and* the full rendered string in memory simultaneously — real memory pressure risk on lower-RAM devices for BADAN's largest possible export.
- **Expected user impact:** Lower peak memory during large exports, reducing OOM/ANR risk on budget devices.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/export/CsvWriter.kt`, `.../export/ExportRunner.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Export
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** A large enough export on a low-RAM device risks an OutOfMemoryError, directly undermining the "raw data is not paywalled" guarantee (large exports must actually complete).
- **Implementation notes:** The checksum computation (`sha256Hex`) would need to switch to a streaming `MessageDigest.update()` call per chunk instead of hashing one final byte array — see PERF-254.

### PERF-253 — JSON export builds domain objects, JSON mirrors, and the final string all in memory at once

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `JsonBundleWriter.data()` maps every domain list to its `@Serializable` JSON-mirror equivalent (`RawSampleJson`, `IntervalRecordJson`, etc.), then serializes the whole `Bundle` in one `JsonCoding.encode()` call — for a full export, domain objects, JSON-mirror objects, and the final JSON string/bytes are all resident in memory simultaneously.
- **Recommendation:** Investigate `kotlinx.serialization`'s streaming JSON encoder (writing directly to an `OutputStream`/`Appendable`) to avoid holding a fully-materialized JSON string for large bundles.
- **Why it matters:** Same class of memory-pressure risk as PERF-252, for the JSON export path specifically.
- **Expected user impact:** Lower peak memory during large JSON exports.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/export/JsonBundleWriter.kt`, `.../export/ExportRunner.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Export
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-252
- **Risk if skipped:** Same risk profile as PERF-252 but for JSON exports specifically.
- **Implementation notes:** `kotlinx.serialization.json.Json.encodeToStream` (JVM target) is the natural fit if available for the project's kotlinx.serialization version.

### PERF-254 — Checksum computed as a second full pass over already-in-memory export bytes

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `ExportRunner.sha256Hex()` runs `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(data)` over the fully-rendered `ByteArray` *after* it's already been built in memory — a second full pass over the same buffer rather than hashing incrementally while writing.
- **Recommendation:** Compute the digest incrementally via `MessageDigest.update()` calls as rows/chunks are written (once PERF-252/253 move to streaming output), avoiding a second full-buffer pass.
- **Why it matters:** Minor CPU cost on its own, but compounds with PERF-252/253's memory-pressure issue since it currently requires the full buffer to exist before hashing can even start.
- **Expected user impact:** Marginally faster large exports; primarily unblocks PERF-252/253's streaming fix.
- **ROI:** 1
- **Importance:** 1
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/export/ExportRunner.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Export
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-252, PERF-253
- **Risk if skipped:** Minor; only worth doing alongside the streaming fixes it depends on.
- **Implementation notes:** Land together with PERF-252/253 rather than as a standalone change.

### PERF-256 — Quality-flag decoding does a linear enum scan per flag per row

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `Rows.readProvenance()` splits the semicolon-joined `quality_flags` string and, for each flag, does `QualityFlag.entries.firstOrNull { it.code == code }` — a linear scan of the enum per flag per row, on every provenance-carrying row read (`raw_samples`, `interval_records`, `sessions`).
- **Recommendation:** Precompute a `Map<String, QualityFlag>` keyed by `code` once (e.g. a companion-object lazy val) instead of a linear `firstOrNull` scan per lookup.
- **Why it matters:** Negligible per call given the small enum size, but it's a free, mechanical fix that compounds with PERF-231's broader "every row pays for every column" pattern.
- **Expected user impact:** Negligible on its own; a clean micro-optimization.
- **ROI:** 1
- **Importance:** 1
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/storage/repositories/RowMapping.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Storage layer
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** None material; lowest priority.
- **Implementation notes:** `private val byCode = QualityFlag.entries.associateBy { it.code }` at file scope.

### PERF-258 — Sensitive-DB log screens re-query data that Home/Timeline already fetched this session

### PERF-261 — HealthConnectAdapter reads constituent record types sequentially instead of concurrently

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `readSamples()` (heart rate, then SpO2) and `readIntervals()` (steps, active energy, distance, resting HR, HRV, respiratory rate — 6 types) each fetch their constituent Health Connect record types one after another inside a single `runBlocking` block, rather than launching them concurrently.
- **Recommendation:** Use `coroutineScope { awaitAll(async { readSteps(range) }, async { readActiveEnergy(range) }, ...) }` for each independent record-type read within `readSamples`/`readIntervals`/`readSessions`.
- **Why it matters:** Each record-type read is an independent IPC/database round-trip to the Health Connect provider; running 6 of them sequentially in `readIntervals` pays the sum of 6 latencies instead of their max.
- **Expected user impact:** Meaningfully faster Health Connect sync, especially for the first 90-day historical pull.
- **ROI:** 4
- **Importance:** 4
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/platform/health/HealthConnectAdapter.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Health Connect integration
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Sync latency scales with the sum of all record-type read times rather than the slowest one, directly hurting the "Connect Health Connect" first-impression flow.
- **Implementation notes:** `readAll()` is already `suspend`, so wrapping the six `readIntervals` calls (and two `readSamples` calls) in `coroutineScope { async { ... } }` is a contained, mechanical change.
- **First patch sketch:** In `readIntervals()`/`readSamples()`, replace the sequential `addAll(readX(range))` calls with `coroutineScope { val a = async { readSteps(range) }; val b = async { readActiveEnergy(range) }; ...; buildList { addAll(a.await()); addAll(b.await()); ... } }`.

### PERF-262 — Paged Health Connect reads fetch pages fully serially with no pipelining

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `HealthConnectAdapter.readAll()`'s paging loop (`do { ... } while (token != null)`) awaits each page's `readRecords` call, appends it, then requests the next page — no overlap between processing page N and fetching page N+1.
- **Recommendation:** Acceptable as-is for typical page counts at MVP data volumes; revisit only if profiling on a user with a very large Health Connect history shows paging as a bottleneck.
- **Why it matters:** Correct and simple; flagged here as a known, accepted tradeoff rather than an active problem, since Health Connect's `ReadRecordsRequest` API doesn't offer an easy way to pipeline pages safely.
- **Expected user impact:** None today.
- **ROI:** 1
- **Importance:** 1
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/platform/health/HealthConnectAdapter.kt` (`readAll`)
- **Affected systems:** Health Connect integration
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-261
- **Risk if skipped:** Low; only matters for users with unusually large Health Connect histories.
- **Implementation notes:** Lowest priority in this cluster — PERF-261's fan-out across record *types* delivers most of the available win; per-type page pipelining is a smaller, riskier follow-on.

### PERF-263 — Every HealthConnectAdapter entry point pays its own runBlocking overhead

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `readSamples`/`readIntervals`/`readSessions` each independently wrap their suspend Health Connect calls in `runBlocking`, rather than the `HealthStorePort` interface itself being `suspend` — so `IngestionPipeline.ingest()` (already running on a background coroutine) pays `runBlocking`'s thread-parking overhead three separate times per sync instead of participating directly in structured concurrency.
- **Recommendation:** Make `HealthStorePort`'s methods `suspend fun`, removing the need for `runBlocking` entirely and letting `IngestionPipeline.ingest()` call them directly (and, per PERF-264, concurrently).
- **Why it matters:** `runBlocking` is specifically discouraged inside code that's already coroutine-based because it can park the underlying thread; three separate instances per sync is avoidable overhead once the port interface is fixed.
- **Expected user impact:** Marginally more efficient thread usage during sync; mainly unblocks PERF-264's fan-out.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/platform/health/HealthStorePort.kt`, `.../platform/health/HealthConnectAdapter.kt`, `.../platform/health/FakeHealthStore.kt`, `.../domain/ingestion/IngestionPipeline.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Health Connect integration / ingestion
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Caps how cleanly PERF-264's read-fan-out can be implemented; not a correctness bug today.
- **Implementation notes:** `FakeHealthStore`'s synchronous implementation would need trivial `suspend` markers too, since it implements the same port.

- **Approval needed:** No

### PERF-269 — Every seed/sync regenerates insights for 4 fixed days, each with its own query set

- **Problem:** `SeedController.seed()` and `AppEnvironment.syncHealthConnect()` both loop `for (dayOffset in 0 until 4)` calling `insightEngine.generate()`, and each call independently queries `intervalRecords` + `latestBaseline` per key metric (3 metrics) — a single sync issues up to 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 additional small queries stacked on top of the ingest/baseline cost already flagged in PERF-205/206/244.

- **Implementation notes:** Land after PERF-244's batched interval-record reads, since `InsightEngine.generate()` could reuse the same batched data instead of querying independently.

### PERF-270 — 90 nights of dedup-plus-write round trips during a single seed

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `DedupLite.reconcile()` itself is cheap and pure, but `IngestionPipeline` calls it once per affected night inside a loop that also does 2-3 DB writes per night (PERF-266) — for a 90-day seed with nightly sleep data, that's up to 90 sequential dedup-plus-write round trips.
- **Recommendation:** Fully addressed by PERF-205's transaction-batching fix; tracked here to make explicit that dedup is a meaningful fraction of first-run seed cost, not just raw ingestion.
- **Why it matters:** Quantifies why the "every night has two overlapping sleep sources" seed-data design (PERF-272) makes first-run cost disproportionately dedup-heavy.
- **Expected user impact:** Same as PERF-205.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/domain/ingestion/IngestionPipeline.kt`, `.../domain/ingestion/DedupLite.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Ingestion / dedup
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-205
- **Risk if skipped:** Same as PERF-205.
- **Implementation notes:** No standalone action needed beyond PERF-205.

### PERF-271 — No incremental/anchor-based Health Connect sync; every sync re-reads the full 90-day range

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `AppEnvironment.syncHealthConnect()` always requests `now - 90 days` to `now` on every manual sync, rather than using Health Connect's changes API or a stored read-anchor — the schema even reserves a `read_anchors` table for exactly this ("Reserved, unused in MVP") but nothing reads or writes it.
- **Recommendation:** Wire up `read_anchors` to Health Connect's changes-token API so a repeat sync only fetches records added/changed since the last successful sync, falling back to the full 90-day range only on first connect.
- **Why it matters:** Every manual "sync" today re-reads and re-upserts up to 90 days of records that mostly already exist (the upserts are idempotent so this is safe, but wasteful) — the single biggest structural fix available for repeat-sync latency.
- **Expected user impact:** Dramatically faster repeat syncs after the first connect.
- **ROI:** 4
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 4
- **Approval needed:** Yes (introduces new sync-state semantics and a new failure mode — anchor invalidation/reset — that affects data-freshness behavior)
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/app/AppEnvironment.kt` (`syncHealthConnect`), `.../platform/health/HealthConnectAdapter.kt`, `.../storage/Schema.kt` (`read_anchors`, already defined)
- **Affected systems:** Health Connect sync
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-206, PERF-261
- **Risk if skipped:** Every sync stays proportional to 90 days of history forever, regardless of how little actually changed since the last sync.
- **Implementation notes:** Health Connect's `HealthConnectClient` exposes a changes-token API (`getChangesToken`/`getChanges`) designed for exactly this; the `read_anchors` table already has the right shape (`store`, `platform_type`, `anchor` BLOB) to store the token.

### PERF-274 — Export history list eagerly decodes the full manifest for every recent job

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `ExportJobRepository.recent()` JSON-decodes the complete `ExportManifest` (including per-metric row counts and file checksums) for all 30 recent jobs every time the Export screen's history list loads, even though the list view likely only needs status/format/row-count/date.

### PERF-275 — No cancellation support for a long-running export

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `ExportRunner.run()` has no `CancellationException`/coroutine-cancellation checks in its loop over up to 44 metrics — a user backing out of `ExportScreen` mid-export still causes the full CPU/IO cost to complete in the background.
- **Recommendation:** Check `coroutineContext.isActive` (or equivalent) periodically in the metric loop so a cancelled coroutine (from navigating away) actually stops the work.
- **Why it matters:** Without this, closing the export screen doesn't free up the device resources the export was consuming, which matters most for the largest ("everything") exports this section already flags as expensive (PERF-246/247/252/253).
- **Expected user impact:** Backing out of an export actually stops the work instead of silently finishing in the background.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/export/ExportRunner.kt`, `.../features/export/ExportScreen.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Export
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Wasted battery/CPU on abandoned exports; not a correctness bug (the job still completes and is recorded).
- **Implementation notes:** Kotlin coroutines cancel cooperatively — a periodic `ensureActive()` call inside the per-metric loop is the standard, low-risk fix.

### PERF-276 — No pre-export size estimate shown to the user

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `ExportScreen` has no way to estimate output size or row count before running an export, so a user has no warning before triggering the expensive "everything" JSON path (PERF-247/253) that this section already identifies as the app's most resource-intensive user-triggered action.

- **Affected systems:** Export

### PERF-277 — No index needed check: ExportRunner's per-source filtering is done in Kotlin post-query

### PERF-279 — No Android CI job exists at all

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` defines only `data-contracts` (JSON validation) and `ios-build-test` jobs — there is no job that builds, tests, or lints the Android module (`apps/android`) at all.
- **Recommendation:** Add an `android-build-test` job (`runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, JDK 17, `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug :app:testDebugUnitTest`) mirroring the iOS job's role.
- **Why it matters:** Build-time regressions, dependency bloat, and unit-test failures in the Android module are currently invisible to CI and only caught by whoever happens to build locally — a direct gap in this repo's build/CI performance posture (a "real gap" the lead auditor already flagged for the assets-sync check; the missing build/test job is the more fundamental version of the same gap).
- **Expected user impact:** Indirect — catches performance/build regressions before they reach `main`.
- **ROI:** 4
- **Importance:** 4
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No (CI-only change, no product behavior)
- **Affected files:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- **Affected systems:** CI/CD
- **Suggested owner:** Infra, Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Every Android-side regression in this audit (build time, R8 config, test failures) ships silently until manually discovered.
- **Implementation notes:** Use `actions/setup-java@v4` (temurin, 17) then `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug :app:testDebugUnitTest --no-daemon`; add Gradle caching in the same change (PERF-283) so the new job isn't slow from day one.
- **First patch sketch:** Add a new job to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with `actions/checkout@v4` + `actions/setup-java@v4` (17, temurin) + `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug :app:testDebugUnitTest` in `apps/android`, gated on the same `push`/`pull_request` triggers as the existing jobs.

### PERF-280 — iOS CI job's xcpretty fallback re-runs the entire build+test suite on any failure

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** The `ios-build-test` job runs `xcodebuild ... test | xcpretty || xcodebuild ... test` — if the piped `xcpretty` run fails for *any* reason (including a single flaky test), the fallback re-executes the full `xcodebuild ... test` a second time from a clean state rather than just re-displaying/parsing the already-captured output.
- **Recommendation:** Replace the `|| xcodebuild ... test` fallback with a non-piping failure path that inspects `xcpretty`'s exit code / the underlying `xcodebuild` exit code directly (e.g. `xcodebuild ... test | tee raw.log | xcpretty; exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}`), so a genuine test failure fails CI once instead of running the entire suite twice.
- **Why it matters:** This doubles CI wall-clock time for the common case of a failing run (which is exactly when engineers are most impatiently waiting on CI), and is pure waste since the second run repeats identical work.
- **Expected user impact:** Faster feedback on failing PRs; lower CI cost.
- **ROI:** 4
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- **Affected systems:** CI/CD
- **Suggested owner:** Infra, Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Every failing iOS CI run costs 2x its actual build+test time indefinitely.
- **Implementation notes:** `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` (bash) correctly captures `xcodebuild`'s exit code even through the `xcpretty` pipe, avoiding the need to rebuild at all.
- **First patch sketch:** In `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `Build & test` step, change the `run:` block to `set -o pipefail; xcodebuild ... test | xcpretty` (a single invocation whose exit status reflects `xcodebuild`'s, via `pipefail`), removing the `|| xcodebuild ... test` fallback entirely.

### PERF-281 — No DerivedData caching across iOS CI runs

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** The `ios-build-test` job has no `actions/cache` step for Xcode's `DerivedData` — every CI run performs a full clean build of the iOS app (~13.7k lines Swift, single module) with no incremental-build carryover from the previous run.
- **Recommendation:** Add `actions/cache@v4` keyed on a hash of `apps/ios/project.yml` + `Package.resolved` (if any) + source-file hash, caching `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData`.
- **Why it matters:** Every CI run pays full clean-build cost even for a one-line change; DerivedData caching is one of the most impactful, lowest-risk CI speed levers available for an Xcode project.
- **Expected user impact:** Faster CI turnaround on every PR.
- **ROI:** 4
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- **Affected systems:** CI/CD
- **Suggested owner:** Infra, Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** CI stays proportional to a full clean build forever, regardless of change size.
- **Implementation notes:** Cache invalidation needs care — a key too broad risks stale/incorrect incremental artifacts masking real build breaks; start with a conservative key (source tree hash) and loosen only if proven safe.
- **First patch sketch:** Add `actions/cache@v4` with `path: ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData` and `key: ${{ runner.os }}-deriveddata-${{ hashFiles('apps/ios/**/*.swift', 'apps/ios/project.yml') }}` immediately after checkout in the `ios-build-test` job.

### PERF-282 — No Homebrew cache for xcodegen install

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** The `ios-build-test` job runs `brew install xcodegen` on every run with no cache — this re-downloads and reinstalls xcodegen (and its dependencies) from scratch every time.

- **Why it matters:** A small but pure-waste cost on every single CI run — xcodegen's version rarely changes between runs.
- **Expected user impact:** Marginally faster CI start time.

- **Affected files:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

- **Risk if skipped:** Small, constant per-run tax; low priority relative to PERF-280/281.
- **Implementation notes:** `macos-15` GitHub-hosted runners may already have some Homebrew packages preinstalled/cached at the image level — worth checking the actual `brew install` timing before investing further here.

### PERF-284 — Gradle configuration cache explicitly disabled

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `apps/android/gradle.properties` sets `org.gradle.configuration-cache=false` explicitly, forgoing Gradle's configuration cache, which reuses the result of the configuration phase across builds.
- **Recommendation:** Flip to `org.gradle.configuration-cache=true` and fix any incompatible plugin usage that surfaces (AGP 8.9.1/Kotlin 2.0.21 both have solid configuration-cache support by this point).
- **Why it matters:** Configuration cache is one of the most effective, low-risk local/CI build-speed wins available in modern Gradle, and this project has explicitly opted out of it.
- **Expected user impact:** Faster local Gradle builds and (once PERF-279/283 land) faster CI builds.
- **ROI:** 4
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/gradle.properties`
- **Affected systems:** Build system
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Every local and CI Gradle invocation re-pays the full configuration-phase cost that configuration cache exists to eliminate.
- **Implementation notes:** Flip the flag and run a full `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug` locally to confirm no plugin incompatibility warnings before committing.
- **First patch sketch:** Change `org.gradle.configuration-cache=false` to `org.gradle.configuration-cache=true` in `apps/android/gradle.properties`, then run `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --configuration-cache` locally and fix any reported incompatibilities.

- **Problem:** `app/build.gradle.kts` applies the `kotlin.compose` plugin but never configures `composeCompiler { reportsDestination = ...; metricsDestination = ...; stabilityConfigurationFile = ... }` — there is no build-time artifact showing which composables/classes the Compose compiler considers unstable or non-skippable.

- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/build.gradle.kts`
- **Affected systems:** Build system / Compose tooling
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** PERF-213/214/228 and similar recomposition findings stay unverified guesses instead of measured facts, and future regressions of the same shape ship unnoticed.
- **Implementation notes:** The Kotlin 2.0 Compose compiler plugin (already applied via `libs.plugins.kotlin.compose`) supports these compiler options directly; no additional dependency needed.
- **First patch sketch:** Add a `composeCompiler { reportsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_reports"); metricsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_metrics") }` block to `apps/android/app/build.gradle.kts`, then run `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug` and inspect the generated `-classes.txt`/`-composables.csv` reports for `HomeData`/`MetricDetailData` stability.

- **Effort:** 3

- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/build.gradle.kts`
- **Affected systems:** Build system / release packaging
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-289

### PERF-289 — Referenced proguard-rules.pro file doesn't actually exist

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** `app/build.gradle.kts`'s `release` block calls `proguardFiles(getDefaultProguardFile(...), "proguard-rules.pro")`, but no `apps/android/app/proguard-rules.pro` file exists in the repo — harmless today only because `isMinifyEnabled = false` means R8 never actually runs.
- **Recommendation:** Create `apps/android/app/proguard-rules.pro` with the keep rules R8 will need (kotlinx.serialization `@Serializable` classes, Health Connect record classes accessed via reflection) *before* PERF-288 enables minification, not after.
- **Why it matters:** Enabling minification (PERF-288) with a missing/empty keep-rules file would silently produce a release build that crashes on reflection-based code paths — this is a landmine for whoever eventually flips `isMinifyEnabled`.
- **Expected user impact:** Prevents a future release-build regression; no change to today's behavior.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 2
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/build.gradle.kts` (no existing `proguard-rules.pro`; new file required)
- **Affected systems:** Build system / release packaging
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** The moment someone enables `isMinifyEnabled = true` (PERF-288) without first authoring this file, release builds silently break on kotlinx.serialization/Health Connect reflection.
- **Implementation notes:** Land this before, not alongside, PERF-288 so the keep rules can be tested independently of the minification flag flip.

### PERF-293 — No Macrobenchmark module to measure and regression-track startup/scroll performance

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** There is no `androidx.benchmark.macro` Macrobenchmark test module anywhere in `apps/android` — nothing quantifies cold/warm start time (`StartupTimingMetric`) or scroll jank (`FrameTimingMetric`) for Home/Timeline, and nothing would catch a regression from a future change.

### PERF-294 — No frame-metrics collection anywhere in the app

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** Nothing in the app integrates `androidx.metrics.performance` (JankStats) or `Window.addOnFrameMetricsAvailableListener` — dropped-frame/jank on Home's scroll, `MetricChart` Canvas redraws, or tab switches is completely invisible in production, with no equivalent to what iOS gets from MetricKit's hitch-rate metrics.

- **Approval needed:** No (local/debug-only instrumentation, no data leaves the device given the "no analytics" constraint)
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/MainActivity.kt` (no existing frame-metrics integration; new code required)
- **Affected systems:** Performance instrumentation
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Jank in production is invisible until a user reports it anecdotally.

### PERF-296 — CI's data-contracts job doesn't validate Android asset mirrors, only iOS

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** The `data-contracts` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` compares `packages/*.json` against the iOS resource mirrors (`apps/ios/Sources/Resources/*.json`) but never checks `apps/android/app/src/main/assets/*.json` against the same source of truth, even though `scripts/sync_android_assets.sh` exists specifically to keep them in sync.
- **Recommendation:** Extend the `data-contracts` job's Python check to also compare each `packages/*.json` file against its Android assets mirror, matching the pattern already used for iOS.
- **Why it matters:** A stale/drifted Android asset (particularly a bloated or malformed `registry.json`) would silently regress the JSON-decode cost flagged in PERF-201 with zero CI signal — the exact kind of gap this audit's startup findings depend on catching early.
- **Expected user impact:** Indirect — prevents silent regressions in the exact JSON assets PERF-201 identifies as a startup cost.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- **Affected systems:** CI/CD / data contracts
- **Suggested owner:** Infra, Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Android asset drift (size or content) is invisible to CI even though the equivalent iOS check already exists.
- **Implementation notes:** The existing Python script in the `data-contracts` job already has the exact dict-comparison pattern needed; add four more `packages/... -> apps/android/app/src/main/assets/...` entries to the same `canonical` mapping.
- **First patch sketch:** In the `data-contracts` job's inline Python script, add the four Android asset paths (`apps/android/app/src/main/assets/{registry,insight_templates,symptoms,csv_columns}.json`) to the existing `canonical` dict alongside the iOS mirrors already checked.

### PERF-297 — No StrictMode enabled in debug builds

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** Nothing in `MainActivity`/the app initializes `StrictMode.ThreadPolicy`/`VmPolicy` for debug builds — the exact main-thread SQLite, SharedPreferences, and asset-decode violations flagged in PERF-201/207/208 would have been caught automatically by `StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.detectDiskReads()/detectDiskWrites()` the moment they were introduced.
- **Recommendation:** Enable `StrictMode` in debug builds (`BuildConfig.DEBUG` guarded) with `detectDiskReads`/`detectDiskWrites`/`detectNetwork` thread policies and a `VmPolicy` that at minimum logs violations.
- **Why it matters:** This is the single cheapest guardrail against every main-thread-I/O finding in this section recurring in the future — a one-time setup cost that pays for itself on the next regression.
- **Expected user impact:** None directly (debug-only); prevents future regressions of the class this audit already found.
- **ROI:** 3
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 1
- **Approval needed:** No
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/MainActivity.kt`
- **Affected systems:** Performance instrumentation / developer tooling
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** PERF-201 (should be enabled after or alongside fixing the current violations, otherwise it will fire immediately and constantly)
- **Risk if skipped:** The exact class of bug this audit spent significant effort finding by hand (PERF-201/207/208) can silently reappear in any future change with no automated warning.
- **Implementation notes:** Enable only in debug builds; a `penaltyLog()` (not `penaltyDeath()`) policy is the safer starting point to avoid crashing QA builds while the existing violations (PERF-201/207/208) are still being fixed.
- **First patch sketch:** Add a `StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder().detectDiskReads().detectDiskWrites().penaltyLog().build())` call guarded by `if (BuildConfig.DEBUG)` at the top of `MainActivity.onCreate`, before `AppEnvironment` is constructed — expect it to fire immediately until PERF-201/207/208 are fixed.

### PERF-298 — No performance-monitoring or ANR-visibility mechanism for production builds

- **Category:** Performance
- **Problem:** Consistent with the architecture-level "no analytics/observability, no crash reporting" gap, there is specifically no performance-monitoring signal (ANR detection, slow-render tracking) of any kind for production Android builds — a production ANR from, say, the unbatched seed path (PERF-205) blocking too long would be invisible post-release.
- **Recommendation:** At minimum, log `ApplicationExitInfo` ANR/crash reasons on next launch (Android's built-in, privacy-neutral API — no third-party SDK required) so developers can retroactively see if a release caused ANRs, without introducing network telemetry that would conflict with the local-first/no-network guardrail.
- **Why it matters:** Without any signal, a real-world performance regression (e.g. PERF-205 blocking long enough to ANR on a low-end device) would only surface through unprompted user complaints, if at all.
- **Expected user impact:** Indirect — faster detection of real-world performance regressions post-release.
- **ROI:** 2
- **Importance:** 3
- **Effort:** 3
- **Approval needed:** Yes (any telemetry, even fully local/on-device, touches the "no analytics/observability" architecture stance and should get explicit product sign-off on scope)
- **Affected files:** `apps/android/app/src/main/java/net/albayyan/badan/MainActivity.kt` (no existing mechanism; new code required)
- **Affected systems:** Performance instrumentation / reliability
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile, Product
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** Production performance regressions (ANRs in particular) are only discoverable via user complaints, with no way to correlate them to a specific release.
- **Implementation notes:** `ApplicationExitInfo.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons()` (API 30+; `minSdk = 26` means this needs a graceful fallback) reads purely on-device with no network transmission, keeping it consistent with the local-first guardrail — but confirm with Product before adding any new persistent logging, even local-only.

## 4. New feature recommendations (300)

## Cluster A — iOS HealthKit real read wiring (currently 100% stubbed)

### FEAT-001 — Build the HKSampleQuery/HKStatisticsCollectionQuery mapping engine

- **Category:** New Feature
- **Problem:** `apps/ios/Sources/Platform/Health/HealthKitAdapter.swift` `readSamples`, `readIntervals`, `readSessions` all return `[]` with a `// TODO: map HK query results to DTOs (post-MVP)` comment — no HealthKit read has ever executed in this app.
- **Recommendation:** Implement `HKSampleQuery`/`HKStatisticsCollectionQuery`/`HKAnchoredObjectQuery` mapping so each method returns real `SampleDTO`/`IntervalDTO`/`SessionDTO` values conforming to `HealthStorePort` exactly as `FakeHealthStore.swift` already does.
- **Why it matters:** `FakeHealthStore` is "the ONLY data source actually used in-app today" — BADAN currently cannot read a single real Apple Health value despite shipping the entitlement strings and a full ingestion pipeline built to receive it.
- **Expected user impact:** Users on iOS get their actual health data instead of permanently seeing 90-day synthetic demo data.
- **ROI:** 5
- **Importance:** 5
- **Effort:** 4
- **Approval needed:** Yes
- **Affected files:** `apps/ios/Sources/Platform/Health/HealthKitAdapter.swift`, `apps/ios/Sources/Platform/Health/HealthStorePort.swift`
- **Affected systems:** iOS health ingestion
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** None
- **Risk if skipped:** The flagship iOS app remains permanently demo-data-only; Android (with its real `HealthConnectAdapter`) is materially ahead in actual functionality.
- **Implementation notes:** Mirror Android's `HealthConnectAdapter.kt` structure (per-metric mapper functions feeding `buildList`) for a consistent bilateral shape.

### FEAT-002 — Wire HealthKitAdapter into AppEnvironment / IngestionPipeline

- **Category:** New Feature
- **Problem:** `grep` for `.ingest(from:` in `apps/ios/Sources` returns exactly one call site — `Sources/App/SeedController.swift:37`, always passed `FakeHealthStore`. `HealthKitAdapter` is never instantiated anywhere in the app.
- **Recommendation:** Add a `healthStore: HealthKitAdapter` property to `AppEnvironment.swift` (mirroring Android's `AppEnvironment.kt:87` `val healthConnect: HealthConnectAdapter by lazy {...}`) and a `syncHealthKit()` method that calls `ingestion.ingest(from: healthStore, range:)`.
- **Why it matters:** Without a DI seam and a call path, FEAT-001's query mapping has nowhere to be invoked from.
- **Expected user impact:** Makes real HealthKit data reachable from the UI at all.
- **ROI:** 5
- **Importance:** 5
- **Effort:** 2
- **Approval needed:** Yes
- **Affected files:** `apps/ios/Sources/App/AppEnvironment.swift`
- **Affected systems:** iOS DI / ingestion
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile
- **Dependencies:** FEAT-001
- **Risk if skipped:** Real read code from FEAT-001 stays dead code with no caller.
- **Implementation notes:** Copy Android's `syncHealthConnect()` shape (`AppEnvironment.kt:94`) including `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` and a `range` of the last 90 days for the first sync.
- **First patch sketch:** Add the lazy `healthStore` property and a `syncHealthKit()` wrapper to `AppEnvironment.swift` that calls the existing `ingestion.ingest(from:range:)`; no query mapping required for this patch alone.

### FEAT-003 — Onboarding "Connect health data" button does not call HealthKit

- **Category:** New Feature
- **Problem:** In `apps/ios/Sources/Features/Onboarding/*.swift` the `connectPrimary` button (line ~296) runs `primaryButton(Self.connectPrimary) { env.completeOnboarding() }` — it never calls `requestAuthorization` or any HealthKit API; the entire "Bring in your health data" onboarding step is decorative.
- **Recommendation:** Wire the button action to call `HealthKitAdapter.requestAuthorization` (via the AppEnvironment seam from FEAT-002), show the system permission sheet, then proceed to `completeOnboarding()` regardless of grant/deny.
- **Why it matters:** This is the single moment users expect the app to actually ask for their health data; right now it silently does nothing while implying it did.
- **Expected user impact:** Onboarding actually results in a working data connection instead of a no-op button.

- **Effort:** 2

- **Affected systems:** iOS onboarding
- **Suggested owner:** Mobile

### FEAT-006 — Map HealthKit sleep stages (HKCategoryValueSleepAnalysis) to SessionDTO/StageDTO

- **Category:** New Feature
- **Problem:** `readSessions` in `HealthKitAdapter.swift` is unimplemented; BADAN's `SessionDTO`/`StageDTO` model (in `HealthStorePort.swift`) already supports deep/REM/light/awake stages exactly as Android's `readSleep` (`HealthConnectAdapter.kt:174-188`) maps them.

### FEAT-007 — Map heartRate quantity samples to SampleDTO

- **Category:** New Feature
